conversation.content:
Good morning, Mama. I’m Dr. Martínez, a perinatal-mental-health clinician here to support new mothers. Over the next few minutes I’d like to use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short—to check how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. This is simply a screening tool; it isn’t a test you can pass or fail, and everything we discuss stays confidential within our care team. We’ll go through ten gentle questions about the past seven days. You can answer in your own words; there are no right or wrong answers, and I’ll never rush you. Ready to start?

Question 1: In the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Good morning, Doctor. [small sigh, half-smile] I… I can still laugh, I guess, but it feels kind of thin. Like, when my sister sent that silly meme yesterday, I chuckled for a second, then it just faded and I felt tired again. Nothing seems really funny the way it used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… that’s pretty much how it’s been. Most of the time it feels like more effort than it’s worth, though.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

[slow exhale] Not really. I mean, I still plan little things—like taking the baby for a walk around the block or meeting my neighbor for coffee—but when the time comes, I just feel… flat, I guess. I do them anyway because I know I should, but that excited buzz I used to get isn’t there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes, yeah. Like yesterday the baby was extra fussy and I kept thinking maybe I ate something that upset her, or I wasn’t holding her the “right” way. My partner said she’s just having a rough day, but I still wondered if I’d done something to cause it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… a few times this week I’ll just be sitting there, everything quiet, and suddenly my chest feels tight, like something bad’s about to happen—even when the baby’s breathing fine and the house is calm. I’ll check her three, four times just to be sure.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not full-on panicky… more like a low-level scared. Like, I’ll be rocking her at 2 a.m. and my heart starts racing out of nowhere, and I have to tell myself, “She’s okay, you’re okay,” until it slows down. It passes, but it’s unsettling while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days feel like one long to-do list I can’t keep up with. I’ll finally get her down for a nap and realize the dishes are still piled up, the laundry’s wet in the washer, and I haven’t eaten. I manage, but by evening I’m just wiped and feel like I’m barely treading water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

I don’t know if it’s being unhappy exactly… more like my mind keeps spinning—did I burp her long enough, is she gaining weight, did I pay the pediatrician bill—so when I finally lie down I can’t shut it off. Takes me forever to drift off, then every squeak from the bassinet jerks me awake.
I have felt sad or miserable

[quiet for a second, then soft voice] Yeah… I get waves of sadness a couple of times a day. Nothing huge, just this heavy feeling that shows up out of nowhere. I’ll be folding her tiny onesies and suddenly feel like crying, even though nothing bad happened. It usually passes if I keep moving.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really… I’ve teared up once or twice, but I haven’t actually cried. I feel kind of numb more than anything, like the tears are stuck.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
[shakes head quickly] No, never. I could never leave my baby like that.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note

Patient-reported symptoms:
- Marked anhedonia: “flat,” effortful laughter, anticipatory tasks completed without prior enjoyment
- Daily waves of sadness, tearfulness without precipitant
- Excessive guilt re infant care; self-blame for routine infant fussiness
- Unprovoked anxiety/tight-chest episodes, nocturnal heart racing, repeated checking on infant
- Overwhelm with daily tasks, “one long to-do list I can’t keep up with”
- Sleep-onset and maintenance difficulties driven by intrusive worries about infant
- Denies current or past self-harm ideation; no suicidal thoughts endorsed

Screening significance:
Persistent low mood, anhedonia, guilt, anxiety, and impaired coping are consistent with probable postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety features. No safety concerns identified today. Recommend formal evaluation with EPDS/PHQ-9 and clinical interview to confirm severity and develop appropriate support plan.
